interviewQuestions.question: What makes mobile touch-target design different from designing clickable elements for a mouse-driven interface?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core difference is precision. A mouse cursor is a single precise point that lands exactly where the user aims it; a thumb covers a soft patch of screen — roughly 40-48 points/dp — and lands imprecisely, especially in real-world conditions like walking or a moving vehicle. That's why both major platforms set explicit minimum touch target sizes: below that size, taps become unreliable not because the element is hard to see, but because it's hard to physically hit.

The part that trips people up is that the **visible** size and the **hit-testing** size can diverge — a button can look comfortably large with generous padding while the actual tappable region is only the inner icon, with the padding excluded from hit-testing. That passes a visual review completely while still missing thumbs constantly in real use, because a developer testing with a mouse in a simulator hits it with pixel precision every time and never reproduces the bug.

Reachability adds a second dimension unique to phones specifically: on a large modern phone held one-handed, the bottom half to two-thirds of the screen is comfortably reachable by thumb, while the top corners require a grip shift. That's a legitimate design signal, not just an ergonomics footnote — primary actions cluster toward the bottom, and reachability difficulty can even be used deliberately to make a destructive action harder to trigger by accident.

**Testing:** whether you understand touch targets as a physical, not just visual, design constraint, and can explain why simulator/mouse testing structurally misses these bugs.

interviewQuestions.question: A support team reports users can't find a feature that's actually already in the app, accessible via a swipe gesture. How would you diagnose and fix this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This pattern — a feature that technically exists but that real users report as "missing" — is the classic signature of a discoverability failure, not a functionality bug, so I'd start by checking whether the feature's only entry point is a gesture with no visible affordance.

Gestures are genuinely great for screen real estate and feel fluid once learned, but they're invisible by default: nothing on screen tells a first-time user that swiping does anything at all, unlike a button, which announces its own existence just by being visible. If that's the root cause here, the support tickets aren't really about the feature being broken — they're about users never discovering the interaction model in the first place, and a percentage of users will simply never find it no matter how long the feature has existed.

The fix isn't necessarily removing the gesture — it's adding a discoverable equivalent alongside it: a menu item, a visible button, or a first-use hint animation that briefly demonstrates the gesture the first few times a relevant screen is shown. I'd also check whether the gesture has any exposed equivalent for screen reader users, since a swipe-only interaction is functionally invisible to someone using TalkBack or VoiceOver regardless of how experienced they are with the app.

The underlying principle for review going forward: a gesture can be an accelerator for power users, but it should never be the *only* path to a feature that matters, because you're implicitly betting that every user will stumble onto or be taught the gesture, and in practice a meaningful fraction never will.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a vague "users can't find this" report to a specific, addressable discoverability gap rather than assuming the feature itself needs to change.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How would you build accessibility testing into a mobile team's workflow so screen-reader gaps get caught before release, not after a complaint?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push for a concrete, repeatable test rather than a checklist review, because accessibility gaps are almost invisible to a sighted code review — a control can look perfectly fine visually while being completely broken for a screen reader user, and reviewers who aren't using the screen reader themselves routinely miss this.

The test I'd standardize: for any new or changed screen, turn on TalkBack or VoiceOver and complete the core flow using only swipe-and-double-tap, no sighted shortcuts, no looking at the screen to infer what's next. This surfaces the real failure modes directly — a custom-drawn control with no accessible label at all, a decorative icon read aloud as noise because it wasn't marked decorative, a label that describes an icon's appearance instead of the action it performs, or a focus order that jumps around the screen in a way that makes no sense read aloud in sequence.

I'd make this part of the actual definition of done for any UI change, not a separate accessibility audit that happens occasionally and separately from normal review — by the time a dedicated audit catches something, it's often shipped for months and the fix competes with new feature work for priority. Catching it at review time costs a few minutes per PR; catching it via a support ticket or an app store accessibility complaint costs a retroactive investigation and a rushed fix.

I'd also specifically flag custom-drawn controls in review, since standard platform widgets get accessibility metadata for free and custom controls don't — that's the single highest-risk pattern for a screen-reader gap, and it's worth calling out explicitly rather than trusting it'll be remembered generically.

**Testing:** whether you can turn "accessibility matters" into an enforceable, low-friction team practice rather than a policy statement nobody actually executes.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Process

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, how would you think about the trade-off between elegant, gesture-heavy UI and accessibility/discoverability, when the design team wants to minimize visible chrome?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd reframe it as a false trade-off in most cases rather than accepting the premise that minimal chrome and accessibility are opposed — the actual conflict is usually "gesture as the *only* path" versus "gesture as an accelerator with a discoverable equivalent," and the second option gets you most of the visual minimalism the design team wants without sacrificing discoverability or accessibility.

Concretely, I'd push the design conversation toward: keep the gesture for power users who've learned it, and add a low-visual-cost discoverable equivalent — a long-press-revealed menu, a subtle first-use hint, or an action exposed through an existing menu that's already part of the chrome — rather than a persistent, chrome-heavy button competing for the same visual minimalism the gesture was meant to preserve. This satisfies the design goal for the common case while giving every user, including screen reader users and first-time users, an actual path to the feature.

Where I'd push back harder is if the proposal has *zero* non-gesture path to a core action — that's the case where the trade-off is real and I'd treat it as a hard no, not a compromise to negotiate, because it means an entire class of users (screen reader users, and any first-time user who doesn't discover the gesture) simply cannot use the feature at all. I'd frame that concretely in terms of who's excluded, not as an abstract accessibility principle, because that's what actually moves a design decision in practice.

The broader point I'd make to the team: accessibility and elegant minimal UI aren't inherently opposed — the tension only shows up when a team treats "discoverable" and "minimal" as mutually exclusive, when in most real designs a small amount of chrome or a well-designed hint can buy back both.

**Testing:** whether you can navigate a real design-versus-accessibility tension with a concrete resolution, rather than either dismissing the design goal or capitulating on accessibility.
